Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Performance across Age Groups: Analysis of 302 700 Examinations.
articles.abstract: Purpose To compare screening digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) performance metrics across age groups. Materials and Methods In this retrospective study, screening mammograms acquired from January 1, 2013, to June 30, 2019, at an academic medical center were reviewed. Each examination included combined digital two-dimensional mammography and DBT and was categorized as true positive, false positive, true negative, or false negative based on 1-year follow-up. Performance metrics were calculated according to Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System definitions and compared across age groups using multivariable generalized estimating equation models. Results Among 93 617 female individuals (mean age, 58 years ± 12 [SD]) who underwent 302 700 DBT examinations, cancer detection rate (CDR) increased with age, from 2.9 per 1000 examinations (208 of 70 549) at ages 40-49 years to 8.3 per 1000 (399 of 48 205) at ages 70-79 years and 10.6 per 1000 (127 of 12 018) at age 80 years and older. Sensitivity increased from 72.5% among those aged 40-49 years to 91.7% among those aged 70-79 years (P < .001). The abnormal interpretation rate (AIR) was highest among those aged 40-49 years (9.3%) and lowest among those aged 80 years and older (5.5%), with corresponding specificities of 91.0% and 95.5% (all P < .001). Positive predictive value (PPV1) increased with age, from 3.2% among those aged 40-49 years to 19.2% among those aged 80 years and older (P < .001). Conclusion Screening DBT performance improved with advancing age, demonstrating higher CDRs, sensitivity, specificity, and PPV1, along with lower AIRs. Keywords: Age, Breast Cancer, Digital Breast Tomosynthesis, Mammography, Screening, Breast See also the commentary by Hussain in this issue. Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA 2026.

articles.title: Deep learning multimodal fusion model based on ultrasound images and clinical-ultrasound texts for differentiating benign and malignant renal tumors.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To develop a deep learning multimodal fusion model based on ultrasound (US) images and clinical-US texts to differentiate benign and malignant renal tumors. METHODS: The retrospective dataset from January 2012 to February 2023 in a tertiary hospital was used for model development and randomly allocated to training and validation sets. An independent prospective test set was obtained from March 2023 to October 2024. We developed Model-G using grayscale US (GUS) images, Model-GC using GUS and color Doppler flow imaging images, Model-T using clinical-US texts, and Model-UT using US images and clinical-US texts. ResNet50 was used for image feature extraction, BERT for text encoding, and ViT for multimodal classification. RESULTS: In total, 1008 patients (740 in training set, 186 validation set, and 82 prospective test set) with a single renal tumor were included. In the validation set, Model-UT achieved the highest diagnostic performance in comparison to Model-G, Model-GC, and Model-T with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.89 (95% CI, 0.86-0.93) (all p-values < 0.05). In the prospective test set, Model-UT yielded an AUC of 0.92 (95% CI, 0.86-0.97), outperforming high-level, mid-level, and low-level radiologists (all p-values < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: The multimodal fusion model presents promising potential in differentiating benign and malignant renal tumors. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Deep learning model integrating US images with clinical-US texts improved benign-versus-malignant renal tumor differentiation. Decision-curve, controlled ablation, and SHAP analyses support its potential use as a clinical decision-support tool.

articles.title: A simple and interpretable method to predict head and neck offline adaptation needs based on anatomical changes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Modern radiotherapy techniques do not automatically account for anatomical changes during treatment, which can lead to reduced target coverage, hotspots, or increased dose to healthy tissues. Adaptive Radiotherapy (ART) addresses this by updating the treatment plan based on the patient's current anatomy. In routine clinical practice, the decision to replan is often triggered by a suboptimal fit of the immobilization mask, identified by the radiation therapy technologist. Because this process is operator dependent and lacks methodological rigor, a quantitative decision-support method could substantially improve the replanning decision. Daily image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) images provide valuable clinical information but often lack sufficient quality for accurate target contouring or reliable dose calculation to support straightforward clinical decision-making. This limitation motivates the need for a simpler, more practical, and scalable alternative. PURPOSE: This study develops an automated workflow to predict the need for replanning at every treatment fraction in head and neck (H&N) cancer patients using robust tools, thus requiring minimal manual validation while aiding the radio-oncologists in their decision-making. METHODS: A retrospective dataset of 21 H&N cancer patients treated on a Tomotherapy Radixact system (Accuray, USA) with kVCT daily imaging was analyzed, of whom 14 underwent replanning during treatment. For each patient, the planning CT (pCT) and daily images were processed in RayStation treatment planning system (RaySearch Laboratories AB, Sweden) via scripts. Rigid registrations were used to align daily images to the pCT, and a patient-specific region of interest (ROI) was defined to consistently capture the same anatomical region across all treatment fractions. ROI volumes were intersected with the external contour and converted to relative volumetric changes with respect to the pCT. By grouping patients according to whether a replanning occurred during treatment, differences in mean volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients were assessed at each treatment fraction. To automatically detect clinically relevant anatomical changes, a simple, interpretable model based on three volumetric features (current volume loss, short-term trend, and long-term trend) was evaluated using cross-validation. Thresholds defining the trigger condition were optimized using a tailored loss function that prioritizes early detection and penalizes false negatives more strongly than false positives. Model variants using different feature subsets and hyperparameters were compared, and the final configuration was selected prioritizing recall, followed by specificity and early flagging. RESULTS: Significant differences in volumetric change between replanned and non-replanned patients emerged at fraction 6 and remained significant for most subsequent fractions. The smallest adjusted p -values occurred around fractions 22-25. Using leave-one-out cross-validation, the best-performing model flagged patients to be replanned with 93% recall, doing so on average 8.4 fractions before clinical intervention. CONCLUSIONS: Consistent differences in local tissue volume loss between replanned and non-replanned patients enabled the development of a simple automated workflow that triggers replanning for offline ART when learned volumetric thresholds are exceeded. This approach provides an objective complement to physician judgement and integrates seamlessly into existing IGRT workflows.

articles.title: Impact of dose reduction and multi-parametric harmonization on multi-organ radiomics robustness in total-body PET imaging: Methodological implications for quantitative theranostics.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Radiomic features derived from positron emission tomography (PET) are sensitive to count statistics and acquisition protocol variability, thereby limiting quantitative reliability in low-dose and multi-center total-body PET imaging. PURPOSE: This study evaluated dose robustness of PET radiomics and assessed the impact of multi-parameter ComBat harmonization on feature reproducibility. METHODS: A multi-center total-body PET dataset comprising 550 patients from two institutions was retrospectively analyzed. Seven dose levels were simulated from list-mode data (Standard; dose reduction factors (DRF) of 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, and 100). Automatic deep learning-based segmentation was applied. A total of 107 Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomic features were extracted from standardized uptake value (SUV)-normalized images. Feature-level ComBat harmonization was performed under five configurations (scanner manufacturer, pixel spacing, radiopharmaceutical, scatter correction, and non-harmonized baseline). Reproducibility was quantified using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC (2,1)) across dose levels, organs, and harmonization settings. RESULTS: Dose reduction produced organ- and feature-dependent effects. Overall, 32.7% of the features achieved good or excellent reproducibility (ICC ≥ 0.75) in at least one anatomical region. Selected first-order and intensity-associated features retained good reproducibility in several anatomical regions under moderate dose reduction (DRF ≤ 20), whereas severe count reduction (DRF 50-100) was associated with greater organ- and feature-dependent instability, particularly among higher-order texture features in vascular and lower-contrast soft-tissue regions. Harmonization produced organ and feature-dependent changes but did not uniformly improve cross-dose reproducibility or compensate for noise-induced instability. CONCLUSION: Radiomics robustness in total-body PET is strongly influenced by dose level, anatomy, and acquisition variability. Moderate dose reduction preserves selected intensity-based features, while extreme count reduction compromises higher-order textures. Harmonization altered reproducibility patterns but did not uniformly improve cross-dose agreement or fully offset noise-induced instability, underscoring the need for dose-aware feature selection in multi-center PET radiomics.

articles.title: Single-time-point renal dosimetry for [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617: Incorporating multi-cycle population data using nonlinear mixed-effects models.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Single-time-point (STP) dosimetry using nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) modeling has emerged as a promising approach, with recent studies demonstrating high accuracy. This framework enables estimation of the time-integrated activity coefficient (TIAC) from a single imaging time point and, consequently, prediction of absorbed dose for subsequent therapy cycles. However, the use of multi-cycle population data to support NLME-based STP dosimetry has not yet been systematically evaluated. PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate whether incorporating multi-cycle population data into an NLME framework improves agreement between STP-derived TIACs and all-time-point (ATP)-derived model-based reference TIACs in renal dosimetry. METHODS: Renal biokinetic data [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 were collected from 10 patients over two therapy cycles, with both kidneys analyzed, yielding 40 renal datasets. In both cycles, SPECT/CT imaging was performed at five time points. A literature-based structural function was used in the NLME modeling to incorporate inter-individual variability, inter-cycle variability, and variability between left and right kidney positions. Goodness-of-fit was evaluated based on visual inspection, relative standard errors (RSEs) < 50%, and the absolute value of the off-diagonal elements in the correlation matrix < 0.8. TIACs derived from ATP fitting were used as the reference (rTIACs). STP fitting was performed using the leave-one-out method across defined scenarios. The TIACs derived from STP fitting were designated as STP TIACs (sTIACs). The accuracy of sTIACs in predicting rTIACs was assessed using relative deviations (RDs) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). RESULTS: The model fits satisfied all predefined goodness-of-fit criteria. STP dosimetry using the multi-cycle dataset offered greater flexibility in time-point combinations, leading to MAPEs < 10%. Additionally, an improvement in early-time-point STP dosimetry was observed when using multi-cycle data. CONCLUSIONS: Incorporating multi-cycle data into NLME-based STP dosimetry reduced extreme RDs, increased flexibility in feasible time-point combinations, and improved early-time-point STP performance in this small two-cycle cohort.

articles.title: Impact of daily machine performance check on prediction models for patient-specific quality assurance of multiple-target stereotactic radiosurgery.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Single-isocenter multiple-target (SIMT) stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivered with standard linear accelerators (linacs) achieves high dose conformity through modulated fields with small multi-leaf collimator (MLC) apertures, making patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA) a critical component of radiotherapy programs. Complexity metrics are established predictors of PSQA results, while daily quality control checks of linacs represent an additional potential source of predictive information. PURPOSE: To investigate whether integrating machine performance check (MPC) parameters with complexity metrics improves machine learning model prediction of the gamma passing rate (GPR) in SIMT SRS PSQA. METHODS: A total of 1054 volumetric modulated arcs from 245 consecutive patients treated with SIMT SRS were included. The median total planning target volume was 5.03 cc (range 0.31-119.65 cc) treated with 10MV-FFF beams in 1 fraction of 20 or 24 Gy, or in 3-5 fractions of 27-32 Gy. PSQA was performed field-by-field using an electronic portal imaging device (EPID) with a gamma criterion of 3%/1 mm and a 95% tolerance limit. Eighteen arc-specific plan complexity metrics (aPCM) and ten MPC features were considered. Feature selection based on hierarchical clustering of the Spearman's rank correlation matrix yielded fourteen features (five aPCM, nine MPC). Data were split chronologically according to the QA session date, with the earliest 80% of arcs used for training and the most recent 20% for testing. Four histogram gradient boosting models were trained to predict the GPR of each arc: model A (aPCM and MPC), model B (aPCM only), model C (MPC only), and model D (MPC predicting the residuals of model B). Model performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Differences between models A and B were assessed with Cohen's f2 and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on residuals. Model explainability was obtained with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). RESULTS: Model A showed the best performance (MAE = 1.7% [1.5, 1.9]; AUC = 0.87 [0.79, 0.93]), closely followed by model B (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.75, 0.89]) and model D (MAE = 1.8% [1.6, 2.0]; AUC = 0.83 [0.76, 0.90]). Model C performed markedly worse, particularly in classification ability (MAE = 2.0% [1.7, 2.2]; AUC = 0.64 [0.58, 0.71]). The incremental effect of adding MPC features was small-to-medium but not significant on residuals (f2 = 0.13 [0.02, 0.27]; Wilcoxon p = 0.213). SHAP identified aPCM as the primary predictors in models A and B, with median MLC gap showing the highest contribution (average absolute SHAP value  | ϕ | ¯   = 1.66%). Among MPC features, couch rotation accuracy showed the highest contribution (  | ϕ | ¯   = 0.27%), considerably smaller than that of aPCM (group mean  | ϕ | ¯   = 0.07% vs. 0.48%). CONCLUSIONS: MPC features did not provide meaningful complementary information for predicting PSQA results of SIMT SRS. Complexity metrics related to MLC aperture characteristics were the dominant predictors, indicating an association between arc complexity and PSQA outcomes in SIMT SRS. To reduce variability in EPID field-by-field PSQA results, we recommend controlling the complexity of SIMT SRS arcs.

articles.title: Dosimetric impact of intrafractional ocular motion in LINAC-based ocular SRS/SRT: Defining real-time eye-tracking thresholds.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Photon-based LINAC ocular stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic radiotherapy (SRS/SRT) offer a noninvasive treatment approach for ocular malignancies. However, intrafractional ocular motion can compromise target coverage because of steep dose gradients and small treatment margins. Although ocular position monitoring and motion-management techniques have been investigated previously, quantitative dosimetric guidance relating angular gaze deviation to target and OAR degradation in modern LINAC ocular SRS/SRT remains limited. PURPOSE: To characterize the dosimetric effects of simulated gaze deviation in photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT, identify planning and geometric factors associated with motion robustness, and derive dosimetrically informed gaze-deviation thresholds for real-time eye tracking. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ninety-eight previously generated photon-based ocular SRS/SRT plans were retrospectively analyzed for ocular motion robustness using an Eclipse scripting approach. Planning target volumes (PTVs) were derived from hybrid CT-MRI and synthetic datasets based on clinically treated plaque brachytherapy cases, with a median PTV of 2.37 cc in the primary cohort. An ocular motion model was developed to simulate gaze deviations from 0° to 30° across 36 sampled directions per deviation level while incorporating both rotational and translational globe motion. All plans were prescribed 25 Gy in one fraction. A total of 109, 368 simulated dose evaluations were analyzed in the primary D95-normalized cohort, with corresponding PTV D98-normalized plans used to evaluate the effect of prescription normalization. Additional paired subgroup analyses evaluated beam energy (6 MV FFF vs. 10 MV FFF), MLC configuration (standard MLC vs micro-MLC), and PTV margin size (2 vs. 1 mm). The primary robustness endpoint was maximum safe gaze deviation, defined using preservation of simulated V100 ≥ 90%. Additional analyses evaluated OAR doses and associations between baseline geometric and dosimetric variables and motion robustness. RESULTS: Target coverage progressively deteriorated with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Using V100 ≥ 90% as the prespecified target-coverage criterion, at least 75% of D95- and D98-normalized plans maintained acceptable worst-direction coverage through approximately 6° and 9°, respectively. Optic nerve D0.03 cm3 increased with gaze deviation, with the 75th percentile remaining at or below 12.1 Gy through approximately 7° for D95-normalized plans and 6° for D98-normalized plans. Lens D0.03 cm3 exceeded the 5-Gy reference threshold in most plans at baseline and was therefore not used to determine a motion threshold. Greater target distance from the globe center strongly predicted reduced motion robustness, whereas larger target volume was associated with greater robustness. Higher plan conformity was also associated with increased motion sensitivity. Beam energy, MLC configuration, PTV margin, and tumor directionality had less practical influence on the derived robustness thresholds. CONCLUSIONS: Photon-based LINAC ocular SRS/SRT demonstrated progressive target-coverage loss and increasing selected OAR doses with increasing simulated gaze deviation. Considering both target coverage and optic nerve dose, an approximately 5° gaze deviation represents a reasonable dosimetrically informed starting point for prospective real-time ocular motion monitoring. Because robustness varied substantially among plans, this value should not be considered a universal clinical threshold, and plan-specific assessment may ultimately support more accurate individualized gaze tolerances.

articles.title: Separation of Anatomical Contributions in MRSI Using a Non-Negative Geographically Weighted Regression Model.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) is a non-invasive neuroimaging tool that maps brain metabolites, providing insights into brain physiology and pathology. However, clinical adoption remains limited due to low spatial resolution and partial volume effects, where acquired signals detect metabolism from different tissue types, preventing clear identification of tissue-specific metabolic patterns. We developed a statistical framework based on non-negative geographically weighted regression (NNGWR) designed to overcome these limitations. The method integrates tissue partial volumes with MRSI data using spatially adaptive regression to interpolate metabolite levels across the imaging volume while separating distinct tissue contributions. Importantly, our model accounts for spatial heterogeneity within tissues rather than assuming metabolic uniformity, providing more physiologically realistic estimates. Simulations using synthetic ground truth data show that our method consistently achieves a lower median absolute percentage error than cubic spline and zero-filling interpolations, especially under high noise or low-resolution conditions. A total of 120 MRSI datasets were acquired at 3 T from a cohort of 36 healthy volunteers to assess predictive performance. To handle real-world data, we implemented a robust reweighting scheme that addresses variable spectral quality by progressively downweighting degraded data rather than discarding it, balancing data retention with model stability. Application to a glioblastoma clinical case demonstrated successful separation of metabolite ratios across healthy, tumour and necrotic tissues. The model identified intratumoural metabolic heterogeneity and provided local confidence for transparent clinical interpretation. By decomposing metabolic contributions by tissue type and accounting for natural spatial variations, the approach enables improved brain tumour characterisation. This model is applicable to other neurological conditions where tissue-specific metabolic alterations serve as disease biomarkers, helping both clinical diagnostics and research into brain pathophysiology.

articles.title: Efficiently harvesting low-energy photons from silicon photon counting detectors.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: X-rays incident on silicon photon counting detectors (Si PCDs) may undergo Compton scattering and deposit only a few keV of energy into the sensor. These events are difficult to distinguish from electronic noise. Prior to reconstruction, the scanner must solve a hybrid estimation problem to determine attenuation, in which the lowest energy bin is corrupted by false counts, but the upper energy bins are essentially immune to electronic noise. PURPOSE: To efficiently estimate attenuation in this hybrid scenario. Prior authors have considered attenuation estimation with PCDs that are fully immune to electronic noise, or in energy-integrating detectors that include electronic noise, but the optimal estimator in the hybrid scenario remains unknown. The purpose of this work is to design such an attenuation estimator that reduces bias and variance in Si-PCD CT images. METHODS: We propose to use convex optimization to build a 2D-lookup table that maps counts using the lowest energy bin (containing false counts) and the upper bins (all counts grouped together as a single bin, free of false counts) to the best estimated object attenuation. The energy thresholds of the Si PCD were selected to be 6 and 10 keV using assumptions from the literature. In the regime of interest, counts are scarce, so both false counts and true counts were modeled as Poisson. Our proposed estimator was compared with three reference estimators: naive logarithm estimator and modified logarithm estimators based on Li et al. (IEEE Trans Med Img 2023) and Bushe et al. (Phys Med Biol 2023). The reference estimators were applied using either both lowest and upper bins, or using upper bins only. 20-, 30- and 40- cm water phantoms, containing two 2.6-cm bone-like inserts, were tested in simulation. We assumed a technique of 120 kVp and 833 mA without mA modulation. To avoid confounding artifacts from beam hardening, the bone-like inserts were modeled as being water-equivalent in atomic number but high density, and a water beam hardening correction was used. RESULTS: The proposed estimator achieved zero average bias and the lowest variance across all phantom sizes when compared to the reference estimators. When using both energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 1, and 1 HU and variances that were 7%, 5%, and 5% higher than the proposed method, respectively, in the area between the two inserts. For the 40-cm phantom, their biases increased to over 20 HU. Conversely, when using only the upper energy bins for the 30-cm phantom, the logarithm, Li's, and Bushe's estimators had biases of 4, 0, and 0 HU but with significant increase in variance to 17%, 14%, and 14% higher than our estimator, respectively, and still produced bias on the 40-cm phantom. CONCLUSIONS: For Si PCDs, setting the lowest energy threshold low enough to detect at least some false counts in combination with our proposed attenuation estimator can improve dose efficiency for non-spectral imaging tasks.

articles.title: Quantifying photon counting detector (PCD) performance using PCD-CT images. Part II. detector spectral response function of clinical scanners.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: An earlier publication, Med. Phys. 52:2796 (2025), reported a method for estimating the mean output counts of photon-counting detectors (PCDs) from reconstructed PCD-CT images. This capability provides a foundation for end users of clinical PCD-CT systems to characterize PCD performance without access to raw data. Building on the previous work, the present manuscript introduces an image-domain approach for characterizing the spectral response function (SRF) of PCDs. The SRF strongly influences the spectral imaging performance of PCD-CT and can vary across PCD-CT platforms, even when the same semiconductor sensor material is used. PURPOSE: To calibrate and validate a theoretical PCD SRF model for a clinical whole-body PCD-CT system (Siemens NAEOTOM Alpha) using DICOM images of physical phantoms. METHODS: PMMA slabs with thicknesses ranging from 1 to 13 inches were placed in the scanner as x-ray spectrum modifiers, while the tube voltage was varied from 70 to 140 kV. The Alpha PCD-CT was operated in static-gantry mode, such that the x-ray spectrum incident on the detector remained static during each scan. The acquired projections were reconstructed by the scanner into DICOM images as if they had been acquired over a full 360  ∘  rotation. For each PCD energy bin, the mean detector output count was estimated from the noise power spectrum of the reconstructed images. Ratios of the estimated mean counts between energy bins were then used to calibrate the free parameters of a theoretical SRF model developed based on the semiconductor material and pixel geometry of the Alpha PCD. This approach is analogous to calibrating a parametric x-ray spectrum model to the actual spectrum of a radiographic or CT imaging system using experimentally measured half-value layers or quarter-value layers. The calibrated SRF model was subsequently validated using PCD-CT energy-bin images acquired under different x-ray spectral conditions generated with copper (Cu) filters (0.5-4.5 mm) instead of PMMA slabs, by comparing the theoretical and experimentally estimated count ratios between energy bins. RESULTS: For the PMMA-based calibration data, the model-predicted total-energy-bin to high-energy-bin count ratios yielded a mean percent error (MPE) of -0.48% (95% CI: [-8.00%, 7.03%]). For the independent Cu-based validation data, the model-predicted count ratios remained in close agreement with the experimental measurements, yielding an MPE of -2.27% (95% CI: [-10.76%, 6.22%]). The calibrated SRF model showed that the mean energy separations between the low-energy and high-energy bins of the Alpha PCD were 10.4, 16.5, 24.4, and 28.7 keV for 70, 90, 120, and 140 kV beams, respectively, indicating greater spectral separation at higher tube voltages. CONCLUSIONS: It is feasible for end users of PCD-CT systems to estimate the SRF from reconstructed images without access to raw detector counts. The estimated Alpha PCD SRF curves are provided in a MATLAB software package, PCD-SPECTRA, which is made available to the research community to facilitate characterization of the spectral performance of PCD-CT systems and support further research and application development.

articles.title: Joint segmentation and landmark detection for cardiac MRI with multi-scale inter-task feature fusion and gradient-bridged anatomical constraints.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Segmentation and landmark detection are essential yet complex tasks in Cardiac MRI (CMR) for quantitative assessment of the heart. Existing automatic CMR analysis methods typically handle the two tasks independently, overlooking their synergies that could improve the performance of both tasks. PURPOSE: To develop an accurate and efficient multi-task learning (MTL) framework that jointly performs segmentation and landmark detection for CMR. METHODS: The proposed SLaDNet-GaB framework integrates a Segmentation and Landmark Detection Network (SLaDNet) with a Gradient-as-Bridge (GaB) loss. SLaDNet adopts a shared feature encoder and two separate decoders to generate segmentation and landmark predictions, respectively. Inter-Task Feature Fusion (ITFF) modules are inserted between the decoders at multiple resolution scales to facilitate bidirectional information exchange via channel-wise attention. Along with two intra-task losses, the dedicated GaB loss is further introduced during training to enforce inter-task anatomical consistency. Specifically, the loss guides the predicted landmarks toward the segmentation objective boundaries using gradient maps. We comprehensively evaluated the proposed method against both single- and MTL baselines on two public CMR datasets: a cine dataset (ACDC; 105/15/30 subjects for training/validation/testing) and a T1 mapping dataset (STONE; 150/20/40 subjects for training/validation/testing). RESULTS: SLaDNet-Gab outperformed the baselines in both segmentation (dice scores: 92.37/94.27% on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05) and landmark detection (point-to-point distances: 2.22/1.51 voxels on ACDC/STONE, p < 0.05). For downstream tasks, the proposed method consistently achieved lower strain and T1 quantification errors than the other methods in most myocardial segments, with per-segment measurements closely agreeing with the manually derived values. Moreover, SLaDNet-GaB demonstrated relatively low training times (11.4/3.2 hours on ACDC/STONE) and an inference time of 6.12 msec./sample suitable for clinical adoption. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed multi-tasking method achieves improved accuracy in CMR segmentation, landmark detection, and downstream quantification, while maintaining high computational efficiency.

articles.title: Real-time intrafraction 3D spine tracking using gantry-mounted kV imaging for single fraction high dose functional radiosurgery.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Spinal nerve root ablation of 70-90 Gy with single fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivered in short partial arcs (30-60 degrees) is an emerging treatment for managing chronic thoracoabdominal wall pain. The proximity of the target to spinal cord and the high per fraction dose demand intrafraction motion monitoring with sub-millimeter accuracy. Pre-treatment cone-beam CT (CBCT) and intermittent room-mounted triggered kV imaging do not provide continuous internal anatomical verification during beam delivery. Gantry-mounted real-time tracking solutions have been mostly validated for full arc stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) at substantially lower doses. PURPOSE: We report comprehensive evaluations of a gantry-mounted, real-time 3D kV spine tracking system based on template matching of continuously acquired fluoroscopic images. Tracking performance was assessed under the demanding conditions of short-arc, high-dose functional SRS. We also present its first clinical use during spinal nerve root ablation for chronic thoracoabdominal wall pain. METHODS: We first performed pre-clinical evaluation with an anthropomorphic spine phantom placed on a programmable motion platform. Tracking performance was evaluated at incremental phantom offsets from -4 to 4 mm and varying arc lengths. The detected shifts were compared to the known offset, as well as estimated shifts from CBCT and room-mounted triggered kV imaging system. Moreover, the tracking accuracy was validated clinically in 12 spine SBRT patients using CBCT projections acquired as part of the routine care. The detected shifts were benchmarked against the CBCT-derived shifts, with offline re-analyses at reduced arc lengths. Finally, under an IRB-approved protocol, the real-time tracking system was deployed as a secondary monitor in two patients (three disease sites) receiving 70 Gy frameless single-fraction SRS to the spinal nerve dorsal roots. We evaluated overall tracking performance and compared the detected shifts in vertebral position to CBCT and room-mounted triggered kV system detected shifts. RESULTS: The phantom study demonstrated an average accuracy of 0.2 ± 0.1 mm (maximum: 0.6 mm) in the detected spine position for offsets up to 4 mm. No substantial impact of the arc length was observed, and the agreement with CBCT and room-mounted triggered kV system was within 0.2 mm. The clinical validation with CBCT data showed an average agreement within 0.4 mm in all directions, with maximum deviations of 0.8 mm. During clinical nerve root ablation treatments, the vertebral body was successfully tracked throughout treatment. Intrafraction motion exceeding 1 mm was detected in 2 of 3 sites by our real-time tracking system, prompting corrective CBCTs and couch shifts. The median (interquartile range) difference in the detected vertebra position compared to room-mounted triggered kV system was -0.2(0.6) mm, 0.1(0.4) mm, and -0.1(0.4) mm in vertical, lateral, and longitudinal directions. CONCLUSION: Our preliminary study demonstrated the feasibility of vertebral body tracking using a real-time 3D kV tracking system during nerve root ablation treatments. Real-time monitoring detected actionable intrafraction motion that prompted couch corrections in 2 of 3 sites, which room-mounted triggered imaging would not have identified until the subsequent arc. This capability might be particularly valuable for short-arc, high-dose treatments, where the window for intrafraction verification is narrow, and the consequence of undetected motion is high.

articles.title: Deep learning for gamma map prediction in breast IMRT verification.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA) in radiotherapy commonly relies on global gamma passing rate (GPR) metrics, which summarize delivery agreement as a single scalar value and therefore provide limited information about the spatial location of dose delivery discrepancies. Spatial prediction of gamma maps may offer a more informative and interpretable representation of PSQA outcomes. PURPOSE: To develop and evaluate a multimodal deep learning framework for predicting two-dimensional gamma maps in breast intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) verification, using portal dose images, multileaf collimator (MLC) modulation maps, and plan complexity metrics. METHODS: A retrospective single-center dataset of 4707 portal dosimetry fields from 644 breast cancer patients treated with IMRT was analyzed. A U-Net-based encoder-decoder architecture was implemented with dedicated encoders for each input modality and intermediate feature fusion before gamma map prediction. The gamma map was predicted as a three-class categorical output (background, failing, and passing) using a softmax layer with per-pixel argmax decoding. Four configurations were compared: portal-only, portal plus modulation maps, portal plus complexity metrics, and fully multimodal input. Five-fold patient-level cross-validation was used to prevent data leakage. Performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis with a 90% GPR threshold, standard classification metrics, GPR agreement within ± 3 %  and ± 5 %  , and a categorical map-level spatial-agreement analysis between predicted and measured gamma maps. RESULTS: Predictive performance improved with multimodal integration. The portal-only model achieved an AUC of 0.77 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71-0.82), whereas the fully multimodal configuration reached 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96); the difference was statistically significant in a paired bootstrap test ( p < 0.001  ). Balanced accuracy increased from 0.64 to 0.77. For the fully multimodal model, 87.9% and 94.6% of cases showed agreement between measured and predicted GPR within ± 3 %  and ± 5 %  , respectively. The categorical map-level spatial agreement was 87.00 % ± 2.08 %  in fields with measured GPR < 90 %  , indicating that the model reproduced the approximate spatial distribution of failing regions. CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal gamma map prediction improved breast IMRT PSQA performance compared with portal-only modeling and extended assessment beyond scalar GPR estimation. By providing spatially resolved predictions of failing regions, the proposed approach may support more informative and interpretable pretreatment QA.

articles.title: Weakly Convex Ridge Regularization for 3D Non-Cartesian MRI Reconstruction.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: While highly accelerated non-Cartesian acquisition protocols significantly reduce scan time, they often entail long reconstruction delays for 3D data. Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can alleviate this, but typically rely on complex, highly parametrized architectures. METHODS: As an alternative, we introduce a rotation-invariant weakly convex ridge regularizer (WCRR). The resulting variational reconstruction approach is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on retrospectively simulated data and out-of-distribution prospective GoLF-SPARKLING and CAIPIRINHA acquisitions. RESULTS: Our approach achieves competitive reconstruction quality while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters and retaining the interpretability of a sparsity-promoting variational prior. CONCLUSION: In summary, WCRR provides a compact and interpretable learned variational prior for 3D non-Cartesian MRI reconstruction.

articles.title: Toward Brain Biosignature at 7 T-Repeatability of a Multiparametric CEST, QSM, QTI, and Sodium Imaging Protocol.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the repeatability of an extended multiparametric 7 T MRI protocol for voxel-wise tissue characterization combining morphological, CEST, QSM, QTI, and Sodium contrasts. METHODS: A repeatability study was performed in 12 volunteers without diagnosed neurological disease on a 7 T MRI system, using a comprehensive acquisition protocol with a combined acquisition time of 45:24 min, from which 45 contrast maps were derived. Quantitative repeatability was assessed using region-based and voxel-wise analyses. Precision and reliability were evaluated using the coefficient of variation (CV), repeatability coefficient (%RC), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Voxel-wise agreement between scan-rescan images was assessed using Pearson correlation coefficients. RESULTS: Across contrasts spanning morphological, CEST, QSM, QTI, and 23Na imaging, %RC was below 20% for 20 contrasts, with mean CV below 5% for most. Repeatability was highest for MP2RAGE T1 maps and QTI MD (CV ≈ 1%-2%; ICC up to 0.86) and lowest for 23Na imaging (ICC < 0.6). CEST contrasts were highly repeatable at low saturation power but more variable at higher power (CV up to ≈8%). QSM contrasts showed moderate ICC (0.46-0.82). Voxel-wise correlations exceeded r = 0.8 for most contrasts, confirming preserved spatial patterns across repeated scans. CONCLUSION: Multiparametric 7 T MRI enables reproducible voxel-wise characterization of brain tissue across a wide range of contrasts. Despite variability in specific contrasts, the overall high repeatability and strong voxel-wise agreement support the feasibility of voxel-wise imaging approaches for quantitative brain imaging and provide a foundation for future applications in clinical research and neuroscience.

articles.title: Letter to the Editor regarding "A multi-centre real-world evaluation of AI-assisted organ at risk contouring on radiotherapy treatment planning workflows".
Filter tilt, dwell time, and IVC diameter in unsuccessful IVC filter retrieval: associations from a single centre experience over ten years.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This retrospective cohort study aims to describe management approaches for inferior vena cava (IVC) filter retrieval and identify independent risk factors for unsuccessful retrieval at our tertiary referral centre. METHODS: All patients who underwent IVC filter insertion at our single tertiary referral centre between February 2016 and August 2025 were included. Kaplan-Meier analysis and a multivariable logistic regression were used to determine rates of retrieval and identify independent risk factors for unsuccessful retrieval. A dedicated database for follow-up of patients with IVC filters was managed by the haematology department. RESULTS: A total of 231 patients were included. 103 of 128 (80.47%) retrievals were successful at the first attempt. The retrieval rates at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year were 59.85%, 72.73%, and 81.06%, respectively. On multivariable logistic regression, filter tilt at insertion (p = 0.016), dwell time (p = 0.009), and smaller IVC diameter (p = 0.030) were identified as independent risk factors for unsuccessful retrieval. CONCLUSIONS: Our follow-up database was instrumental in scheduling early removal and minimising loss to follow-up to achieve high retrieval rates. We advocate for the early removal of filters to maximise successful retrieval, avoid the need for advanced removal techniques, and prevent long-term complications. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Our findings support hypotheses that prolonged dwell time and greater tilt lead to unsuccessful retrieval and we additionally identify smaller IVC diameter as a previously unreported risk factor. Practically, we provide strong evidence to support the use of a prospectively managed follow-up database for filters.

articles.title: Mind the data: pitfalls and perspectives in acquiring and interpreting preclinical evidence for the FLASH effect.
articles.abstract: FLASH radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) has rapidly emerged as a promising approach to widen the therapeutic window through differential sparing of normal tissue. However, despite substantial experimental activity, uncertainties remain regarding the magnitude, reproducibility, and determinants of the FLASH effect. This work reviews common pitfalls and sources of ambiguity in the acquisition and interpretation of preclinical FLASH data to support clinical application. In particular, the widespread use of fixed single-dose study designs, over-reliance on differential endpoint-based metrics, and limited quantification of effect size may obscure the true magnitude and clinical relevance of observed effects. Moreover, small dose-modifying effects are highly susceptible to experimental and biological variability, including dosimetric uncertainties, endpoint sensitivity, and environmental factors such as oxygenation. Heterogeneity in experimental protocols and endpoints further complicates cross-study comparisons. Addressing these challenges through improved quantitative characterisation, harmonised methodologies, and transparent reporting will be essential to enable robust interpretation and support the clinical translation of FLASH-RT.

articles.title: Toward rapid MR-based assessment of osteoporosis in the lumbar spine - Acceleration of IR-UTE imaging for bound water quantification in trabecular bone at 1.5 T.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to explore the feasibility of accelerating inversion recovery-prepared ultra-short echo time (IR-UTE)-based bound water (BW) quantification in trabecular bone of lumbar vertebrae at 1.5 T. METHODS: A 3D radial IR-UTE sequence for selective BW imaging at 1.5 T was implemented using Pulseq to acquire data from the lumbar spine in seven young healthy volunteers and three patients with osteoporosis (OP). Reconstructions from seven reference datasets (30-min acquisition time) and retrospectively undersampled subsets (acceleration factor R = 6) derived therefrom were subsequently paired, yielding 126 input-target pairs for fine-tuning a denoising convolutional neural network (DnCNN) pre-trained on IR-UTE images of the knee. Scalar image quality metrics were calculated, and trabecular BW proton density (BWPD) in L1-L4 was determined using the remaining datasets from two young healthy volunteers and one patient with OP, including an additional prospectively accelerated scan in one healthy volunteer. RESULTS: Applying the DnCNN enhanced agreement with the reference, as indicated by improved scalar image metrics and reduced bias in BWPD values. Trabecular BWPD, thus derived, was higher in the young healthy volunteers than in the patient with OP (mean across L1-L4 [mol 1H/L]: 2.307 and 2.378, the latter 2.384 prospectively, vs. 0.664). CONCLUSION: BW quantification in lumbar spine trabecular bone using IR-UTE at 1.5 T is feasible, and BWPD values differed between the evaluated young healthy volunteers and the patient with OP. Transfer learning via DnCNN fine-tuning demonstrated the potential to accelerate IR-UTE-based BW analysis in trabecular bone while preserving agreement with reference acquisitions.

articles.title: Association of whole-body dixon MRI-derived abnormal bone marrow volume with prognosis in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate whether imaging parameters derived from whole-body Dixon MRI are associated with prognosis in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (MM). METHODS: This retrospective study included 123 patients with newly diagnosed MM who underwent whole-body MRI. A deep learning model was used to segment bone marrow in major regions. Abnormal bone marrow was defined using region-, age-, and sex-specific lower fat fraction (FF) thresholds from a community population. Total, axial, and peripheral abnormal bone marrow volumes and FFs were extracted. Associations with clinical parameters and stages were assessed by Spearman's correlation and group comparisons. Prognostic values were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression. RESULTS: Abnormal bone marrow volumes correlated negatively with hemoglobin and albumin and positively with β2-microglobulin, M protein, and bone marrow plasma cell percentage (|ρ| = 0.19-0.53; p < 0.05). Abnormal volumes differed across stages (p < 0.05), whereas FFs did not. Total abnormal bone marrow volume ≥ 122.4 cm3 was independently associated with overall survival (OS) (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.71, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.31-5.58, p = 0.007) and progression-free survival (PFS) (HR = 1.88, 95% CI = 1.10-3.24, p = 0.022). Axial abnormal bone marrow volume ≥ 93.0 cm3 was independently associated with OS (HR = 2.15, 95% CI = 1.07-4.32, p = 0.032) and PFS (HR = 1.85, 95% CI = 1.07-3.21, p = 0.028). CONCLUSION: Whole-body Dixon MRI-derived abnormal marrow volume was independently associated with OS and PFS in MM, suggesting its potential utility in prognostic assessment.

articles.title: Denoising of multi b-value diffusion-weighted MR imaging using an improved non-local means filter.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) maps derived from the quantitative analysis of multiple b-value diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) has shown many clinical applications. However, DW-MRI is affected by Rician noise, which compromises the reliability of IVIM maps. METHOD: To address this issue, we propose an improved non-local means (NLM) filtering method that utilizes a prior image to improve the estimation of similarity weights. Moreover, the proposed method is implemented using a fast version of NLM filtering to efficiently perform image denoising. We used both simulated and real DW-MRI data to evaluate the performance of the proposed method and compared the results with those obtained using three image denoising methods: local principal component analysis, Marchenko-Pastur principal component analysis, and pre-filtered rotationally invariant non-local principal component analysis. RESULTS: Results from the simulated DW-MRI data showed that the proposed method outperformed the other three methods in terms of root mean-squared error and improved the quality of IVIM maps. Results from the real DW-MRI data showed that the proposed method yielded IVIM parameter values consistent with those reported in the literature and exhibited lower coefficients of variation compared to the other three methods. CONCLUSION: Overall, the proposed NLM filtering method has the potential to be a fast and reliable denoising technique for multiple b-value DW-MRI.

articles.title: Preoperative breast cancer subtyping using multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging and explainable machine learning.
articles.abstract: Breast cancer exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity with distinct molecular subtypes that differ markedly in prognosis, treatment response, and clinical management. To enable imaging-based subtype differentiation, this study retrospectively analyzed suspected breast cancer patients who underwent breast MRI between September 2020 and September 2024, finally including 292 breast cancer lesion records from 283 patients with postoperative IHC-confirmed subtypes. All patients received SyMRI, DCE-MRI, and DWI. Quantitative metrics were extracted-pre- and post-contrast T1, T2, and PD values, T1-Ratio, and PD-Ratio, ADC, TIC patterns, BI-RADS categories, and morphological features. Elastic-net logistic regression was embedded within the training folds for feature selection, and five machine-learning classifiers-LR, SVM, KNN, RF, and DT-were evaluated using the historical internal test set and repeated patient-grouped nested cross-validation. After false-discovery-rate adjustment, ADC-Tumor, post-contrast T1, post-contrast T2, T1-Ratio, and Burr sign differed significantly across molecular subtypes. Repeated patient-grouped nested validation selected the random-forest model (macro-average one-vs-rest AUC, 0.946 ± 0.035), which achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.789-0.927) in the historical internal test set; class-specific results and confusion matrices were reported with uncertainty intervals. TreeSHAP analysis of the selected random-forest model identified post-contrast T1 (overall mean absolute SHAP, 0.053), post-contrast T2 (0.053), and T1-Ratio (0.050) as the leading overall contributors, with distinct subtype-specific patterns. These findings support further investigation of multiparametric breast MRI as a preliminary adjunct for preoperative subtype assessment; the model cannot replace histopathological and IHC confirmation and requires independent external validation.

articles.title: Incidental T1-hypointense spinal lesions: Retrospective application of Bone-RADS.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Incidental T1-hypointense bone lesions on spinal MRI frequently prompt follow-up. We retrospectively applied the 2022 Society of Skeletal Radiology Bone Reporting and Data System (Bone-RADS) framework to a historical cohort to assess concordance between observed lesion outcomes and Bone-RADS expectations and quantify imaging that would not have been recommended under the framework. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study was approved by the institutional Research Ethics Board with waiver of informed consent. Spine MRI reports from May 2013 to May 2023 were reviewed. Of 256,989 spine MRI examinations, 6709 reports contained the term "T1-hypointense," and 276 patients with recommended and completed lesion-directed follow-up met inclusion criteria. Bone-RADS was applied retrospectively to this follow-up-enriched cohort; no histopathological reference standard was available. RESULTS: Among 276 patients with incidental T1-hypointense bone lesions, 212 had solitary lesions eligible for retrospective Bone-RADS classification and 64 had multiple lesions, which were not classified. Of the 212, 186 were classified as Bone-RADS 1 and 26 as Bone-RADS 2/3. The 186 Bone-RADS 1 patients underwent 295 lesion-directed follow-up examinations that would not have been recommended under retrospective application of Bone-RADS. No lesion developed aggressive features or required biopsy or intervention. Median follow-up for Bone-RADS 1 lesions was 5.5 months (interquartile range, 3.0-21.5 months). CONCLUSION: Observed outcomes were concordant with Bone-RADS expectations but do not constitute validation of the framework. Retrospective application identified follow-up examinations beyond Bone-RADS recommendations for lesions classified as Bone-RADS 1. Prospective multicenter evaluation against histopathological or long-term clinical reference standards is required.

articles.title: Contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM)-guided biopsies: Initial experience at a tertiary cancer center.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM)-guided biopsy is an emerging technique with little data available. Our purpose is to determine the imaging features and predictors of malignancy for CEM-guided biopsies. METHODS: IRB-approved, HIPAA-compliant search of our institutional database identified CEM-guided biopsies performed from January 1, 2023 to October 4, 2024. The electronic medical record, images, procedure and pathology reports were reviewed for patient demographics, biopsy target characteristics and available pathology. Descriptive statistics were performed. RESULTS: 53 CEM-guided biopsies were performed during the study period. The median patient age at biopsy was 50 years (range 34-87 years). The median biopsy target size was 1.2 cm (range 0.4-9.3). Biopsy targets included non-mass enhancement (36/53, 67.9%; average size 1.8 cm, range 0.4-7.0 cm), mass (14/53, 26.4%; average size 1.2 cm, range 0.4-4.3 cm), asymmetry (2/53, 3.8%; average size 2.2 cm, range 0.5-3.8 cm), and architectural distortion (1/53, 1.9%; size 9.3 cm). Fifteen of 53 (28.3%, 95% CI 17.6-41.9%) biopsied targets yielded malignancy, 4 of 53 (7.5%) yielded high-risk pathology, and 34 of 53 (64.2%) yielded benign pathology. One high-risk lesion and one benign discordant biopsy site yielded malignancy on excision. Post-biopsy hematomas occurred in two patients, none requiring intervention. No statistically significant predictors of malignancy were identified. CONCLUSION: In our single-institution study, CEM-guided biopsy is an effective technique to sample suspicious enhancing breast findings, yielding malignancy in a quarter of cases.
